item.title: Best Podcasts for Personal Growth: 12 Shows Worth Your Time
item.description: Looking for the best podcasts for personal growth? These 12 shows deliver real, actionable advice on habits, mindset, money, and relationships.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

I used to think I didn’t have time for podcasts. Then I did the math: my commute, my dog walks, and my dishwashing duty added up to roughly ten hours a week. Ten hours of dead air I was spending on nothing in particular.

That was three years ago. Since then, podcasts have replaced mindless scrolling in my daily routine, and a handful of shows have genuinely changed how I handle my mornings, my money, and my anxiety. Not in a vague, inspirational-poster way — in a “here’s a specific technique I tried on Tuesday” way.

If you’re looking for the best podcasts for personal growth, this list is for you. I’ve skipped the obvious fluff and focused on shows that give you something concrete: a framework, a habit, a question to sit with. Here are twelve worth your earbuds, organized by what you’re actually trying to improve.

How I Picked These Shows

A few ground rules. Every podcast here:

  • Delivers actionable content. You can finish an episode and do something differently the same day.
  • Has staying power. These aren’t shows that burned bright for six episodes. They’ve built real catalogs.
  • Respects your time. Most episodes run 30–60 minutes. A couple are longer, but they earn it.

One tip before you start: don’t binge five new shows at once. Pick one, listen to three episodes, and actually apply something. Growth comes from implementation, not consumption.

Best Podcasts for Building Better Habits

The Habit Coach with Ashdin Doctor

If you’ve ever abandoned a habit by day four, this show is for you. Ashdin Doctor keeps episodes short — often under 15 minutes — and focuses on tiny, sustainable changes rather than dramatic overhauls. One episode that stuck with me was about “habit stacking”: attaching a new habit to something you already do automatically. I started doing ten push-ups right after brushing my teeth. Six months later, it’s just part of my night.

Hidden Brain

Hosted by journalist Shankar Vedantam, Hidden Brain explores the psychology behind our behavior. It’s not a self-help show in the traditional sense, but it might be more useful because of that. Episodes on procrastination, willpower, and why we sabotage our own goals give you the “why” behind your patterns. Understanding the mechanism makes the fix a lot easier.

Best Podcasts for Mindset and Mental Clarity

The One You Feed

Named after a Cherokee parable about two wolves — one representing negative thoughts, one positive — this show is a long-running conversation about managing your inner life. Host Eric Zimmer interviews psychologists, authors, and teachers about anxiety, resilience, and self-compassion. It’s gentle without being saccharine, and it’s especially good for anyone who struggles with overthinking.

Ten Percent Happier with Dan Harris

Dan Harris started this show after a panic attack on live television led him to meditation. The premise: you don’t need to be a monk to benefit from mindfulness. He’s a recovering skeptic, which makes him a great guide for other skeptics. Start with his conversations with meditation teachers or the episodes on handling difficult emotions.

Best Podcasts for Career and Money Growth

The Tim Ferriss Show

Tim Ferriss is often credited with popularizing the long-form interview format, and his show remains one of the best. He deconstructs world-class performers — athletes, investors, authors — to find the routines and tools they actually use. Episodes run long, so use the show notes to find topics that matter to you. His recurring question, “What would this look like if it were easy?”, has saved me from overcomplicating more projects than I can count.

Afford Anything

Hosted by Paula Pant, this show blends personal finance with lifestyle design. The core idea: you can afford anything, but not everything. Every dollar and every hour is a trade-off. Paula’s episodes on frugality without misery and on building income streams are practical and refreshingly free of get-rich-quick energy.

The Career Contessa Podcast

If you’re navigating a job change, a promotion, or a toxic workplace, this one’s for you. Host Lauren McGoodwin covers salary negotiation, burnout, and career pivots with real interviews from women who’ve done it. The salary negotiation episodes alone are worth a listen before your next review.

Best Podcasts for Relationships and Communication

Where Should We Begin? with Esther Perel

This one is different: you listen to real couples in therapy sessions (anonymized, with consent). It sounds voyeuristic, but it’s actually a masterclass in communication. Even if you’re single, the patterns Esther Perel identifies — how we fight, how we avoid, how we ask for what we need — apply to every relationship in your life.

We Can Do Hard Things

Glennon Doyle, her sister Amanda, and her wife Abby Wambach tackle the hard stuff: boundaries, grief, friendship, self-worth. It feels like sitting in on a wise, funny conversation between people who genuinely care about each other. The episodes on setting boundaries changed how I handle family obligations.

Best Podcasts for Big-Picture Thinking

On Being with Krista Tippett

This is the show I recommend when someone wants to think about meaning, not just productivity. Krista Tippett interviews poets, scientists, and spiritual leaders about what it means to be human. It’s slow and thoughtful — the opposite of a hustle culture podcast — and that’s exactly the point.

The Knowledge Project with Shane Parrish

Shane Parrish interviews thinkers and decision-makers about mental models: the frameworks we use to make better choices. Episodes on clear thinking and on learning how to learn are standouts. If you like the idea of upgrading your decision-making the way you’d upgrade a computer, start here.

How to Actually Get Value From These Shows

Listening is the easy part. Here’s how to make it stick:

  1. Take one note per episode. Just one idea you want to remember. I keep a running note on my phone titled “Podcast Ideas.”
  2. Apply within 48 hours. Pick one small action and do it before the memory fades.
  3. Use playback speed wisely. 1.25x is fine for interviews. Don’t crank it to 2x and wonder why nothing sticks.
  4. Skip episodes freely. You don’t owe any host your full attention. If an episode isn’t landing, move on.
  5. Revisit favorites. Some episodes hit differently a year later. I’ve re-listened to the same Esther Perel episode three times.

Final Thoughts

The best podcasts for personal growth aren’t the ones with the most downloads — they’re the ones that meet you where you are. If you’re rebuilding your habits, start with The Habit Coach. If you’re wrestling with your mindset, try The One You Feed. If you want to think bigger, queue up On Being.

Pick one show from this list this week. Listen to a single episode during a walk or your commute. Then do one thing differently because of it. That’s the whole formula — and it works better than any binge-listening session ever will.

item.title: Digital Detox Challenge: 7 Tips That Actually Work
item.description: Tired of doomscrolling? Learn how to run a digital detox challenge with practical tips, real schedules, and strategies that stick long after day seven.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

The first time I tried a digital detox, I lasted four hours. I had downloaded a screen-time app, deleted Instagram, and announced to my family that I was “unplugging for a week.” By lunch, I was checking email on my laptop because I’d convinced myself it didn’t count.

That’s the thing nobody tells you about digital detoxes: the hardest part isn’t the technology. It’s the negotiation you run with yourself. Your brain is remarkably good at finding loopholes—the laptop doesn’t count, checking the weather doesn’t count, “just one quick look” doesn’t count.

A digital detox challenge works better when you stop treating it as an act of willpower and start treating it as a design problem. You’re not fighting your phone. You’re redesigning your day so the phone becomes less relevant.

Here’s what actually works, based on research on habit formation, attention, and the experiences of people who’ve made this stick.

Why a Challenge Beats a Vague Intention

“Spend less time on my phone” is not a goal. It has no finish line, no rules, and no way to know if you’ve succeeded. A challenge has all three.

Behavioral research consistently shows that specific, time-bound commitments outperform open-ended ones. A 7-day or 14-day structure gives you a container. You know when it starts, you know when it ends, and you can measure whether you did it. That clarity is what turns a vague wish into an actual behavior change.

It also gives you an exit ramp. A permanent detox sounds like a punishment. A 10-day challenge sounds like an experiment. Experiments are easier to start.

Tip 1: Define Your Detox by Category, Not by Device

The most common mistake is declaring war on “screens.” Screens are how you work, navigate, pay bills, and talk to your grandmother. Banning them entirely is unrealistic and sets you up to fail.

Instead, pick specific categories to cut:

  • Passive scrolling (social feeds, short-form video, news aggregators)
  • Notifications (all non-human ones)
  • Reactive communication (checking messages the moment they arrive)
  • Comfort checking (picking up your phone with no purpose)

You can keep maps, banking, and calls. You’re not a monk. You’re just removing the behaviors that leave you feeling drained rather than informed or connected.

A friend of mine did a 14-day challenge where the only rule was “no phone in the first hour after waking and the last hour before bed.” That’s it. She reported better sleep within four days. Narrow rules are easier to keep and often deliver outsized results.

Tip 2: Run a Two-Day Baseline Before You Start

Don’t guess how much time you spend on your phone. Measure it.

For two days before your challenge begins, track your actual usage without changing anything. Most phones have this built in. Note:

  • Total daily screen time
  • Your top three most-used apps
  • How many times you pick up your phone
  • How you feel after your heaviest usage window

This baseline does two things. It gives you a real number to compare against later, and it often delivers a small shock. Seeing “4 hours 12 minutes” in cold data hits differently than a vague sense of “I’m on my phone too much.”

Tip 3: Build Friction Into Your Devices

Willpower is unreliable. Friction is reliable.

The goal is to make the unwanted behavior take three extra seconds. That’s usually enough to break the automatic reach.

Practical friction moves:

  • Move social apps off your home screen. Put them in a folder on the second page, or delete them and use the browser version only.
  • Turn your phone to grayscale. Color is a major driver of engagement. A gray feed is noticeably less compelling.
  • Log out after each use. Typing a password every time is a natural speed bump.
  • Charge your phone outside the bedroom. Buy a $12 alarm clock. This single change eliminates the most common late-night and early-morning scroll sessions.
  • Turn off all non-human notifications. Your bank doesn’t need to interrupt you. Neither does a shopping app.

None of these require discipline. They just require ten minutes of setup.

Tip 4: Replace, Don’t Just Remove

Here’s where most detoxes collapse. You remove the phone, and suddenly there’s a void. Boredom rushes in, and boredom is the fastest route back to the thing you’re trying to avoid.

You need a replacement behavior ready before the craving hits. Not a list of “things I could do”—an actual plan for the specific moments when you’d normally reach for your phone.

Map your triggers to replacements:

Trigger Old Behavior Replacement
Morning coffee Scroll news Read 5 pages of a book
Waiting in line Check social Look around, breathe, or listen to a podcast
Lunch break Watch shorts Walk outside for 10 minutes
Boredom at 9pm Endless scrolling Board game, journal, or call a friend
Anxious moment Comfort check Write down the worry in one sentence

Keep this list somewhere visible for the first few days. After a week, the replacements start to feel normal.

Tip 5: Tell People What You’re Doing

A detox in secret is a detox you can quietly abandon.

Tell your household, your close friends, and anyone who regularly messages you. Something simple: “I’m doing a 10-day digital detox. I’ll still answer calls and texts, but I’m off social media until the 15th.”

This does three things. It creates social accountability. It sets expectations so nobody thinks you’re ignoring them. And it often recruits an ally—someone who’ll check in and ask how it’s going.

One caveat: don’t turn it into a performance. Announcing your detox on the platform you’re detoxing from defeats the purpose. Keep it to people who actually matter in your daily life.

Tip 6: Plan for the Hard Moments in Advance

Days 2 and 3 are usually the worst. The novelty has worn off, the habit loop is screaming, and your brain is producing very convincing arguments about why you should just check one thing.

Write down your response to those arguments before they arrive. A single sentence works: “I’m not quitting, I’m just not doing it right now.”

Also decide in advance what happens if you slip. Not if—when. Because you probably will.

The rule should be: a slip is data, not failure. If you check Instagram on day 4, note what triggered it, adjust your friction, and continue. The people who finish challenges aren’t the ones who never slip. They’re the ones who don’t use a slip as permission to quit.

Tip 7: End With a Review, Not a Return

The last day of your challenge isn’t the finish line. It’s the moment you decide what to keep.

Sit down and answer three questions:

  1. What did I not miss at all? These are things you can cut permanently.
  2. What did I genuinely miss? These are worth reintroducing—on your terms.
  3. What replaced the scrolling, and did I like it? Keep those replacements.

Most people find that one or two apps were providing almost no value, while one or two were genuinely useful for connection. The goal isn’t zero technology. It’s intentional technology.

Consider setting permanent rules from your findings: no phone at the dinner table, no social apps before 9am, a weekly 24-hour break. Small, permanent boundaries beat dramatic one-time cleanses.

A Realistic 7-Day Starter Plan

If you want a structure to follow, try this:

  • Day 1: Baseline measurement. No changes yet.
  • Day 2: Remove social apps from your home screen. Turn off non-human notifications.
  • Day 3: No phone for the first hour after waking.
  • Day 4: No phone for the last hour before bed. Charge it outside the bedroom.
  • Day 5: One full meal per day with no devices at the table.
  • Day 6: Take a two-hour block and do something offline—a walk, a hobby, a project.
  • Day 7: Review. Decide what stays and what goes.

It’s not extreme. That’s the point. A challenge you complete is worth more than a challenge you abandon on day two.

The Takeaway

A digital detox isn’t about proving you can live without your phone. It’s about noticing how much of your attention you’ve handed over without deciding to. The challenge is just a way to look at that honestly.

Start small. Build friction. Replace the habit instead of just deleting it. And when you slip—because you will—treat it as information rather than failure.

Your attention is the most valuable thing you own. A week is a reasonable amount of time to check who’s been spending it.

item.title: How to Organize Your Digital Life (Without Losing Your Mind)
item.description: Feeling buried by files, photos, and passwords? Here's a practical system to organize your digital life in a weekend—and keep it that way.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Last month, a friend spent three hours searching for a single PDF. It was her apartment lease—needed for a mortgage application—and it existed somewhere across four email accounts, two old laptops, and a phone she’d replaced in 2022. She found it eventually. In her Downloads folder. Named scan_0043.pdf.

Most of us aren’t that far behind. We’ve accumulated a decade of digital clutter: 14,000 unsorted photos, three cloud drives, passwords saved in a notes app, and a browser with 47 open tabs we’re “definitely going to read later.”

The good news? You don’t need a complicated productivity system or a weekend retreat to fix this. You need a few decisions, made once, and about four hours of focused effort. Here’s how to actually do it.

Start With the Three Questions

Before you touch a single file, answer these:

  1. Where does everything live? Pick one primary cloud service (Google Drive, iCloud, Dropbox—whatever you already pay for) and one place for photos. Everything else becomes a temporary holding zone.
  2. What do you actually need to keep? Be honest. You will never re-read that 2016 conference agenda.
  3. How often will you maintain this? A system you can’t sustain is worse than no system. Fifteen minutes every Sunday beats a heroic annual cleanup.

Write your answers down. This is your constitution—every future decision gets measured against it.

Step 1: Consolidate Your Storage

The average person now juggles files across at least three services, plus local drives. That fragmentation is the root cause of most digital chaos.

Do this:

  • Choose your primary drive. Move active documents there.
  • Designate one archive location—an external hard drive or a cheap cloud tier—for things you need to keep but rarely open (tax returns, old projects).
  • Delete duplicate cloud accounts. If you haven’t opened a service in six months, download your data and close it.

One warning: don’t try to merge everything in a single afternoon. Move one category at a time—documents first, then photos, then media. You’ll quit halfway if you attempt it all at once.

Step 2: Build a Folder Structure You’ll Actually Use

Most people’s folder systems collapse because they’re either too complex or too vague. A folder called “Stuff” tells you nothing. A folder called “2024/Q3/Invoices/Vendor_A/Final/v2” is a part-time job.

A structure that works:

Documents/
  Finance/
  Health/
  Home/
  Work/
  Personal/
Archive/
  Taxes/
  Old Projects/

Five to seven top-level folders, maximum. Go one or two levels deep—no more. If you’re tempted to create a fourth level, you probably need a better file name instead.

On naming files: Use YYYY-MM-DD_description for anything dated. 2024-03-15_lease_agreement.pdf sorts chronologically and tells you what it is at a glance. This one habit eliminates most future searching.

Step 3: Tame the Photo Avalanche

Photos are where digital organization goes to die. We take 20 a day and organize zero.

You have two realistic options:

Option A: Lean on search and AI. Google Photos and Apple Photos both recognize faces, places, and objects. If your photos are already uploaded, you can largely stop organizing manually and just search “beach 2022” when needed.

Option B: Monthly albums. Once a month, spend ten minutes creating an album for that month’s best 20–30 photos. Delete the rest—screenshots, accidental bursts, blurry duplicates. Over a year, that’s 300 curated photos instead of 6,000 random ones.

Most people should do a hybrid: use automatic backup for everything, but curate a “Favorites” album quarterly for the shots that actually matter.

Step 4: Fix Your Passwords Once and For All

If your passwords live in your head, a notes app, or a spreadsheet named passwords.xlsx, stop reading and fix this today. It’s the single highest-leverage hour you’ll spend.

  • Get a password manager. Bitwarden (free), 1Password, or your browser’s built-in manager. Any of them beats what you’re doing now.
  • Change your email password first. It’s the master key to everything else.
  • Turn on two-factor authentication for email, banking, and social accounts.

You’ll never memorize a password again, and you’ll stop reusing the same one across twelve sites—which is how most accounts actually get compromised.

Step 5: Declutter Your Digital Surfaces

Files and passwords are half the battle. The other half is everything you look at daily.

Email: Unsubscribe from five newsletters this week. Use filters to auto-sort receipts and notifications into folders you check weekly, not hourly. Inbox zero is optional; a manageable inbox is not.

Phone home screen: Keep only apps you use daily. Everything else goes into folders or off the first screen entirely. You’ll pick up your phone less without even trying.

Browser tabs: Install a session manager like OneTab, or simply bookmark what matters and close the rest. Those 47 tabs are costing you RAM and attention.

Subscriptions: Check your app store and bank statements for recurring charges. The average household pays for 4–5 services it barely uses. Cancel two.

Step 6: The 15-Minute Weekly Reset

This is the part everyone skips, and it’s why systems collapse. Once a week—Sunday evening works for most people—do this:

  • Empty your Downloads folder (file what matters, delete the rest)
  • Clear your desktop
  • Process any loose papers by scanning them into your primary drive
  • Delete screenshots you don’t need
  • Glance at your subscriptions and inbox

Fifteen minutes. Set a timer. When it goes off, you’re done.

A Realistic Timeline

You won’t fix ten years of clutter in one sitting, and you don’t need to. Here’s a sane schedule:

  • Week 1: Set up your password manager and consolidate cloud storage.
  • Week 2: Build your folder structure and sort documents.
  • Week 3: Tackle photos—backup first, then curate.
  • Week 4: Declutter email, phone, and subscriptions.
  • Ongoing: The weekly 15-minute reset.

A month from now, you’ll find that lease in thirty seconds instead of three hours. And more importantly, you’ll stop dreading the moment you need to find anything at all.

The goal isn’t a perfectly empty inbox or a color-coded folder tree. It’s a digital life that works quietly in the background—so you can spend your attention on things that actually matter.

item.title: How to Organize Digital Photos: A Stress-Free System
item.description: Overwhelmed by thousands of camera roll photos? Learn a simple, sustainable system to organize, back up, and actually enjoy your digital memories again.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

My phone once warned me that I had 47,000 photos. Forty-seven thousand. Somewhere in that pile were my daughter’s first steps, a trip to Iceland, and roughly 3,000 screenshots of recipes I’ll never make. Finding anything meant scrolling through years of visual noise.

If that sounds familiar, you’re not alone. The average person takes hundreds of photos a month and organizes almost none of them. But here’s the good news: you don’t need a complicated system or expensive software. You need a simple routine that takes about 15 minutes a week. This is the exact system I use now — and it actually sticks.

Why Your Photos Get Out of Control

The problem isn’t you. It’s the design of modern phones. Every photo gets dumped into one endless stream, and there’s no natural moment where you’re forced to sort anything. Add in duplicates from burst shots, screenshots, and photos your friends text you, and the mess compounds fast.

The fix isn’t a one-time marathon cleanup. It’s building a habit that prevents the backlog from ever forming again.

The Three-Bucket System

Before you touch a single file, understand this: every photo you own belongs in one of three buckets.

Bucket 1: Keep. Genuinely meaningful photos — family, milestones, travel, friends. These get organized and backed up.

Bucket 2: Reference. Screenshots, receipts, serial numbers, recipes, document photos. These get sorted into a folder or app, not your photo library.

Bucket 3: Delete. Blurry shots, accidental pocket photos, duplicates, the seventeenth version of the same sunset. These go.

Most people’s libraries are 60% Bucket 3. That’s why it feels so overwhelming — you’re trying to organize clutter instead of clearing it first.

Step 1: Do a First Pass (The 80/20 Cleanup)

Don’t try to perfect your entire library in one weekend. Instead, set a timer for 30 minutes and go through your most recent 500 photos. Delete anything blurry, duplicated, or meaningless. You’ll likely cut that batch in half.

Repeat this a few times over a couple of weeks rather than trying to do 47,000 photos at once. Progress beats perfection.

A quick tip: On iPhone, open Photos, tap Albums, then scroll to Duplicates. Android users can use the Files by Google app to find similar images. Clearing duplicates alone often removes thousands of files in minutes.

Step 2: Build a Folder Structure That Makes Sense

Once you’ve cleared the junk, you need somewhere for the keepers to live. The best structure is boring and predictable. Mine looks like this:

  • Photos → 2024 → 2024-06 Vacation – Oregon Coast
  • Photos → 2024 → 2024-12 Holidays
  • Photos → Family → Kids

Two rules make this work:

Use date-first naming. Starting folders with the year and month (2024-06) keeps everything in chronological order automatically. No more hunting through alphabetical chaos.

Name by event, not by date alone. “2024-06 Vacation – Oregon Coast” tells you everything. “IMG_4821” tells you nothing.

You don’t need dozens of folders. Three levels deep is plenty: Year → Event → (optional) sub-event.

Step 3: Pick One Home Base

Your photos should live in one primary place, not scattered across your phone, laptop, three cloud services, and an old external drive. Choose one:

  • Apple Photos or Google Photos if you want automatic syncing and face recognition.
  • A cloud drive like Dropbox, OneDrive, or iCloud if you prefer folders you control manually.
  • A local drive plus cloud backup if you’re privacy-focused and don’t mind a bit of manual work.

The tool matters less than the commitment. Pick one, move everything there, and stop hedging.

Step 4: Back Up With the 3-2-1 Rule

This is the part everyone skips until a hard drive dies. The 3-2-1 rule is simple and worth following:

  • 3 copies of your photos
  • 2 different types of storage (e.g., cloud + external drive)
  • 1 copy off-site (cloud counts, or a drive at a relative’s house)

For most people, this means: photos on your computer or phone, backed up to the cloud, plus a yearly copy on an external hard drive that lives somewhere else. That’s it. Set it and forget it.

Step 5: The 15-Minute Weekly Routine

The system only works if you maintain it. Here’s the routine that keeps my library clean:

Every Sunday, 15 minutes:

  1. Open your camera roll and delete obvious junk from the past week.
  2. Move screenshots and receipts to a “Reference” folder or app.
  3. Drop any standout photos into their event folder.

That’s it. Fifteen minutes a week prevents the 47,000-photo problem from ever coming back. It’s the digital equivalent of doing dishes nightly instead of letting them pile up for a month.

Step 6: Actually Enjoy Your Photos

Here’s the part people forget: organizing photos isn’t the goal. Enjoying them is. Once your library is clean, do something with it:

  • Create a yearly photo book. One book per year, 50-100 favorite photos. It takes an evening and becomes a family heirloom.
  • Set up a digital frame. A Wi-Fi frame in the kitchen that rotates through recent favorites turns your archive into daily joy.
  • Make a shared album. Send vacation photos to the friends who were there. It takes two minutes and people love it.

A photo you never look at is just a file. A photo you print, share, or display is a memory.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Don’t rely on “sorting it later.” Later never comes. Sort in small batches as you go.

Don’t over-categorize. If you have 400 folders, you’ve built a maze, not a system. Keep it simple.

Don’t skip the backup. Organizing photos that aren’t backed up is like folding laundry in a house with no roof.

Don’t delete aggressively without checking. When in doubt, keep it. Storage is cheap; regret isn’t.

Start Today, Not Someday

You don’t need to fix 47,000 photos this weekend. You need to spend 30 minutes today clearing your most recent batch, create three folders, and set a weekly reminder. That’s the whole system.

Six months from now, you’ll open your photo library and feel something unusual: calm. And when your kid asks to see pictures from that beach trip, you’ll find them in ten seconds instead of ten minutes.

Start with the last 100 photos on your phone. Right now. Your future self will thank you.

item.title: Meal Planning Apps Review: 5 Best Options Tested
item.description: We tested 5 top meal planning apps for budget, dietary needs, and time. See which ones actually save you money and stress each week.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

I spent three months paying for meal planning apps so you don’t have to. My goal was simple: figure out which ones actually reduce the 5 p.m. “what’s for dinner” panic and which ones just look pretty in the App Store.

The results surprised me. Two apps cut my grocery bill by roughly $60 a month. One was so frustrating I deleted it after a week. And the cheapest option turned out to be the best fit for my household.

Here’s what I found, plus how to pick the right app for your situation.

What Actually Matters in a Meal Planning App

Before the reviews, let’s set the criteria. Most “best of” lists rank apps by features, but features don’t matter if you won’t use them. I graded each app on four things:

  • Recipe quality. Do the meals taste good, or do they read like they were written by someone who’s never cooked?
  • Grocery list accuracy. Does the list match what the recipes need, or are you double-buying onions every week?
  • Time to plan. If it takes 45 minutes to plan a week, you’ll quit by week three.
  • Cost. Both the subscription price and whether the app actually saves you money at the store.

The 5 Apps I Tested

1. Mealime — Best for Beginners

Mealime is the app I recommend to anyone who says “I don’t cook.” You pick your dietary preferences (vegetarian, low-carb, gluten-free), choose meals from a weekly list, and it builds your grocery list automatically.

What worked: Recipes are genuinely simple. Most take under 30 minutes, and the instructions assume zero technique. The free version covers everything a beginner needs. I made a lemon-herb chicken with roasted vegetables in 25 minutes on a Tuesday night, and my picky 9-year-old ate it.

What didn’t: The recipe pool gets repetitive after about six weeks. You’ll see the same stir-fry variations. The Pro version ($5.99/month) adds more recipes but isn’t essential.

Verdict: Start here if you’re new to meal planning. Free tier is genuinely usable.

2. Paprika — Best for People Who Already Love Recipes

Paprika isn’t a meal planning service. It’s a recipe manager that happens to have excellent planning tools. You clip recipes from any website, and Paprika strips out the life story and saves just the ingredients and steps.

What worked: This solved my biggest problem — I had recipes scattered across bookmarks, screenshots, and Pinterest boards. Paprika pulled them all into one place. The grocery list combines ingredients across recipes, so if three meals need garlic, it tells you to buy three cloves total, not three bulbs.

What didn’t: There’s no recipe library. You bring your own. If you don’t already collect recipes, this app has nothing to offer you. It’s also a one-time $4.99 purchase, which is either a steal or a waste depending on how you cook.

Verdict: Perfect for the home cook with a recipe hoarding habit. Useless for everyone else.

3. eMeals — Best for Budget-Conscious Families

eMeals partners with grocery stores like Walmart and Kroger. You pick a plan (budget-friendly, keto, kid-friendly, and about 15 others), and it generates a week of meals plus a shopping list sorted by store aisle.

What worked: The budget plan was the real winner. Meals averaged $2.50 per serving, and the app estimated my total grocery cost before I left the house. I spent $112 on a week of dinners for four people — about $25 less than my usual unplanned trip.

What didn’t: The store integration is hit-or-miss. Walmart worked well; my local grocery chain didn’t support it, so I had to shop manually. And at $9.99/month, it’s the priciest option here.

Verdict: Worth it if you shop at a supported store and feed a family. Skip it if you cook for one or two.

4. Samsung Food (formerly Whisk) — Best Free Option

Samsung Food is free, and it does about 80% of what the paid apps do. You save recipes, build shopping lists, and share plans with family members.

What worked: The collaborative feature is genuinely useful. My partner and I both added meals to the same weekly plan, and the grocery list updated in real time. No more texting “did you buy eggs?”

What didn’t: The recipe discovery is weak. Search results skew toward food blog content of varying quality, and there’s no curation. You need to know what you want to cook before you open the app.

Verdict: The best free option. Great if you already have recipes and just need organization.

5. PlateJoy — Best for Dietary Restrictions

PlateJoy builds meal plans around your specific health needs — diabetes-friendly, low-FODMAP, vegan, and more. It asks detailed questions about your goals and generates a personalized plan.

What worked: The personalization is real, not marketing fluff. When I set it to “high protein, no dairy,” every single recipe complied. For anyone managing a medical condition through diet, this is a genuine relief.

What didn’t: The $12.99/month price is steep, and the recipes are functional rather than exciting. You’re paying for precision, not pleasure.

Verdict: Worth it if you have real dietary constraints. Overkill otherwise.

How to Choose Without Wasting Money

Here’s the shortcut version:

  • You’re new to cooking: Mealime (free)
  • You hoard recipes: Paprika ($4.99 once)
  • You feed a family on a budget: eMeals ($9.99/month)
  • You want free and simple: Samsung Food
  • You have dietary restrictions: PlateJoy ($12.99/month)

Three Tips That Made Every App Work Better

Plan for five dinners, not seven. Something always comes up — leftovers, a late meeting, a takeout craving. Planning seven meals means throwing food away. Five is realistic.

Shop your pantry first. Before finalizing any list, check what you already have. Every app will happily sell you a third jar of cumin.

Do a 15-minute Sunday reset. Open the app, pick meals, approve the list, done. The people who fail at meal planning are the ones who try to do it “whenever they have time.” They never do.

The Bottom Line

The best meal planning app is the one you’ll actually open on Sunday afternoon. For most people, that’s a free app with a simple interface, not a $13/month service with 40 features you’ll never touch.

Start free. Upgrade only when you hit a real limitation. And if you try one for two weeks and it feels like a chore, delete it and try another. The whole point is to make dinner easier, not to add another subscription to manage.

item.title: The 7-Day Digital Detox Challenge: Reclaim Your Focus
item.description: Feeling burnt out by screens? Take the 7-day digital detox challenge to reset your attention, improve sleep, and reconnect with real life.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Last Tuesday, I watched a friend try to read a paperback at a coffee shop. In eleven minutes, she picked up her phone four times. She wasn’t waiting for anything urgent. There was no crisis. Her hand just moved on its own, like a reflex she’d lost control over.

That moment stuck with me, because I recognized it. Most of us have a version of that story. The average person now checks their phone within five minutes of waking up and touches it over 2,000 times a day. We’re not choosing to be on our devices that often. We’re reacting to them.

A digital detox challenge is a structured way to break that reflex. Not a permanent vow of silence from technology, but a short, deliberate reset that shows you what your attention feels like when it belongs to you again.

This guide walks you through a realistic 7-day plan, the science behind why it works, and how to make the benefits last after day seven.

Why a Digital Detox Actually Works

Your brain isn’t designed for this

Your attention system evolved for a world of scarcity — a few important signals, long stretches of quiet. Modern apps are engineered for the opposite. Variable rewards, infinite scroll, and push notifications all trigger dopamine loops that keep you checking “just one more time.”

A detox doesn’t “cleanse” you in any mystical sense. What it does is interrupt the cue-response cycle long enough for your brain to stop expecting a hit every few minutes.

The real benefits show up fast

Research on short-term screen reduction consistently points to a few quick wins:

  • Better sleep — less blue light and mental stimulation before bed
  • Improved focus — your baseline attention span starts to recover within days
  • Lower anxiety — fewer comparisons and doom-scroll sessions
  • More presence — you actually notice meals, conversations, and walks

Most people feel a noticeable shift by day three or four.

The 7-Day Digital Detox Challenge

Here’s the structure. You don’t need to be perfect. You need to be intentional.

Day 1: Audit, don’t change

Before you cut anything, measure it. Check your phone’s screen time report. Write down your top three most-used apps and your daily average. No judgment — just data.

Action step: Screenshot your weekly screen time and set it as your phone wallpaper for the week. It’s a surprisingly effective reality check.

Day 2: Kill the noise

Turn off every non-essential notification. Social media, news, shopping apps, games — all of them. Keep calls, messages from actual humans, and calendar alerts.

Action step: Go to settings and disable notifications app by app. This takes ten minutes and changes everything.

Day 3: No phone for the first and last hour

Your morning and evening are the two most vulnerable windows. Scrolling in bed wrecks sleep. Scrolling at breakfast hijacks your focus before the day starts.

Action step: Charge your phone outside the bedroom. Use a cheap alarm clock. In the morning, don’t touch the phone until you’ve eaten, showered, or stepped outside.

Day 4: A full social media fast

One day. No Instagram, TikTok, X, Facebook, or whatever your poison is. Delete the apps from your phone for the day if that helps. You can reinstall tomorrow.

Action step: Replace the habit with something physical — a walk, stretching, cooking something from scratch. Your hands need a job.

Day 5: Single-tasking day

No phone while watching TV. No scrolling while eating. No second screen during meetings. One thing at a time.

Action step: Put your phone in another room during meals and focused work blocks. Notice how strange the quiet feels at first.

Day 6: The analog afternoon

Spend a full afternoon doing something that has nothing to do with a screen. Read a book, work in the garden, play a board game, take a long walk with a friend.

Action step: Leave your phone at home if you can. If you can’t, put it on airplane mode in your bag.

Day 7: Reflect and design your new normal

Look back at the week. What was hard? What was surprisingly easy? What did you actually miss, and what did you not miss at all?

Action step: Write down three rules you want to keep going forward. Examples: no phone at the dinner table, no social media before 9 a.m., phone charges outside the bedroom.

Common Pitfalls (and How to Dodge Them)

Going too extreme

A 30-day silent retreat sounds impressive, but most people quit by day two. Seven days is short enough to commit to and long enough to feel a difference.

Replacing one screen with another

If you quit Instagram and spend the week binge-watching Netflix, you haven’t detoxed. You’ve just switched channels. Swap screen time for something embodied — movement, conversation, nature, making things.

Treating it as punishment

This isn’t about guilt. It’s about curiosity. You’re running an experiment to see how you feel when the input dials down. Approach it like a scientist, not a penitent.

Skipping the “after” plan

The detox is the easy part. The hard part is not sliding back into old patterns by Thursday of the following week. That’s why day seven matters so much.

How to Make It Stick

A few habits that help the reset last:

  • Keep one “no-phone zone” in your home — usually the bedroom or the dinner table
  • Set app timers for your two biggest time sinks
  • Do a mini-detox one weekend a month
  • Tell someone what you’re doing so they can hold you to it
  • Notice the wins — better sleep, calmer mornings, real conversations — and let them reinforce the change

You don’t need to become a person who lives in a cabin without Wi-Fi. You just need to be the one holding the wheel.

Final Thoughts

The point of a digital detox challenge isn’t to hate technology. It’s to stop letting technology make all your decisions for you. Seven days is enough to feel the difference — clearer mornings, longer attention, fewer phantom phone checks.

Start tomorrow. Pick one rule from day one and go. Your brain will thank you by Wednesday.

item.title: Create a Personal Budget That Actually Works (Step by Step)
item.description: Stop the paycheck-to-paycheck cycle. Learn how to build a realistic budget that fits your lifestyle, with actionable steps and real examples.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: Create a Personal Budget That Actually Works (Step by Step) DESCRIPTION: Stop the paycheck-to-paycheck cycle. Learn how to build a realistic budget that fits your lifestyle, with actionable steps and real examples. TAGS: personal budget, money management, budgeting tips, financial planning, lifestyle

Introduction

I once sat at my kitchen table, staring at a spreadsheet that told me I had $47 left for the next two weeks. The problem? I’d already spent $200 on takeout the week before. The budget wasn’t broken—I was. I had created a plan that looked good on paper but ignored how I actually lived.

Most people fail at budgeting not because they lack discipline, but because they design a system that fights their real spending habits. A budget isn’t a punishment. It’s a tool that gives you permission to spend on what matters while cutting waste you don’t notice. In this guide, I’ll walk you through the exact process I’ve used to build a budget that survived job changes, surprise car repairs, and yes—that impulsive coffee habit.

Why Most Budgets Fail (And How to Avoid It)

Traditional budgeting advice tells you to track every penny, cut all luxury, and save 50% of your income. That works for about three weeks. Then you feel deprived, binge on a weekend trip, and give up entirely.

The real reason budgets fail: they’re too rigid. Life is messy. Your budget needs room for birthdays, flat tires, and the occasional pizza delivery when you’re too tired to cook.

The fix: Build a flexible framework, not a prison. A budget that works accounts for three things: fixed costs, variable essentials, and guilt-free fun. If you try to eliminate fun entirely, you’ll rebel. Give yourself a small “no questions asked” category from day one.

Step 1: Know Exactly What You Earn (The Real Number)

Before you can spend wisely, you need your true income. Not your salary. Your take-home pay.

Write down your monthly after-tax income. If you’re paid bi-weekly, multiply your paycheck by 2.17 (since some months have three paydays) to get an average. If you’re self-employed or have variable hours, use your lowest-earning month from the past year as your baseline. This prevents you from budgeting money you haven’t earned yet.

Example: Sarah earns $3,200 per month after taxes, but her side hustle brings in an extra $400 on good months. She budgets based on $3,200 and treats the extra as a bonus for savings or debt.

Step 2: Track Your Spending for 30 Days (Don’t Judge Yet)

You can’t fix what you don’t see. For one month, track every single dollar you spend. Use a free app like Mint or YNAB, a simple spreadsheet, or even a notebook. The method doesn’t matter. The honesty does.

Include that $4.50 latte. The late fee you forgot. The cash you handed your kid for the school book fair. This isn’t about shame—it’s about data.

What you’ll discover: Most people find that 10-20% of their income goes to small, recurring expenses they barely notice. That’s your low-hanging fruit.

Step 3: Separate Needs from Wants (Be Brutally Honest)

Now look at your tracked spending and split it into three categories:

  • Fixed necessities: Rent, utilities, minimum debt payments, insurance, groceries (not takeout), transportation to work.
  • Variable necessities: Gas, medical bills, basic clothing replacements, childcare.
  • Discretionary: Streaming services, dining out, hobbies, new clothes, gifts, subscriptions.

The trap: We convince ourselves that wants are needs. “I need Netflix to relax after work.” No, you need rest. You can get that from a walk or a library book. Be honest about what you’d actually cut if you lost your job tomorrow.

Step 4: Choose Your Budgeting Method (One Size Does Not Fit All)

There are three proven methods. Pick the one that matches your personality.

The 50/30/20 Rule (Best for beginners)

  • 50% to needs (rent, food, utilities, minimum debt)
  • 30% to wants (dining, travel, hobbies)
  • 20% to savings and debt repayment

This works if you don’t want to track every category. Just make sure your needs don’t exceed 50%. If they do, you need to adjust your housing or transportation.

Zero-Based Budgeting (Best for detail-oriented people)

Every dollar of income is assigned a job. If you earn $3,000, you allocate $3,000 to expenses, savings, and debt. At the end of the month, your balance is zero (not in a bad way—you’ve told every dollar where to go).

Example:

  • Rent: $1,000
  • Groceries: $400
  • Utilities: $200
  • Savings: $300
  • Debt: $200
  • Fun: $200
  • Misc: $200
    Total: $2,500 (with $500 left to assign—maybe to an emergency fund or a vacation goal)

The Envelope System (Best for overspenders)

Withdraw cash for categories where you tend to overspend (dining, entertainment, clothing). Put the cash in labeled envelopes. When the envelope is empty, you stop spending in that category. It hurts to hand over physical cash, which makes you think twice.

Pro tip: You don’t need envelopes for everything. Use this only for your weakest categories.

Step 5: Build an Emergency Fund First (Before Anything Else)

A budget without an emergency fund is a house on sand. If your car breaks down or you get sick, your budget collapses.

Start with $1,000 as a mini emergency fund. Then aim for 3-6 months of basic expenses. Keep this in a separate high-yield savings account, not your checking account.

How to fund it: Treat it like a bill. Set up an automatic transfer of $50 or $100 on payday. You won’t miss what you don’t see.

Real example: When my friend Jake’s water heater burst, his $1,200 emergency fund covered the deductible. He didn’t touch his credit card. That’s the peace of mind a budget provides.

Step 6: Automate Everything You Can

Willpower is a limited resource. Don’t rely on it. Automate your savings, bills, and debt payments so you never have to decide to pay them.

  • Set up automatic transfers to savings on payday.
  • Enroll in autopay for rent, utilities, and credit cards (minimum at least).
  • Use a separate account for discretionary spending.

Why this works: When money moves out of your checking account before you can spend it, you adapt quickly. You learn to live on what’s left.

Step 7: Review and Adjust Monthly (It’s a Living Document)

Your budget isn’t carved in stone. Review it once a month. Did you overspend on groceries? Maybe you need a higher grocery budget and a lower dining-out budget. Did you save more than expected? Put it toward a goal.

The monthly review checklist:

  1. Compare actual spending to your plan.
  2. Identify one category to improve next month (not all of them).
  3. Adjust your allocations if your life changed (new job, new baby, new hobby).
  4. Celebrate progress. If you saved $50 more than last month, that’s a win.

Real-World Example: How One Budget Changed a Life

Let me tell you about Maria. She earned $2,800 a month and always felt broke. She was making car payments, paying student loans, and eating out four times a week. After tracking her spending, she realized she spent $350 a month on restaurants.

She didn’t cut it all out. She dropped to twice a week ($175) and used the saved $175 to start an emergency fund. Six months later, she had $1,050 saved. She then put that $175 toward her student loans. Her debt payoff timeline shrank by two years.

The lesson: Small, sustainable changes beat dramatic overhauls every time.

Common Pitfalls (And How to Dodge Them)

  • “I’ll start next month.” No, you won’t. Start today with one small action: write down your income and your top three fixed expenses.
  • “I don’t make enough to save.” Everyone can save something. Even $10 a week builds to $520 a year. It’s not about the amount—it’s about the habit.
  • “Budgeting is too restrictive.” A budget gives you freedom. It tells you, “Yes, you can go out to dinner Friday night because you already planned for it.”
  • “I’ll just use an app.” Apps are tools, not solutions. You still need to look at the numbers and make decisions.

Final Thoughts: The Budget That Works Is the One You Keep

A perfect budget you abandon is worthless. An imperfect budget you stick with for six months will change your financial life. Start simple. Give yourself grace. Adjust as you go.

Your budget should feel like a pair of well-worn jeans—comfortable, familiar, and just right for your life. Not a straightjacket.

Your next step: Open a spreadsheet or grab a notebook. Write down your income. List your top five fixed expenses. That’s it. Tomorrow, do the next small thing.

The goal isn’t perfection. It’s progress. And you’ve already made the first step by reading this far. Now go make it real.

item.title: Smart Tech Side Hustles to Boost Your Income in 2025
item.description: Discover profitable tech side hustle ideas with real examples and actionable steps. From freelancing to digital products, start earning today.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: Smart Tech Side Hustles to Boost Your Income in 2025 DESCRIPTION: Discover profitable tech side hustle ideas with real examples and actionable steps. From freelancing to digital products, start earning today. TAGS: tech side hustles, make money online, freelance tech work, passive income tech, lifestyle

Introduction

Last year, I watched a friend quit his corporate marketing job after his side hustle—building simple automation scripts for local real estate agents—started paying his rent twice over. He didn’t have a computer science degree. He just saw a boring, repetitive task and figured out how to kill it with a few lines of code.

That’s the beauty of tech side hustles today. You don’t need to be a Silicon Valley engineer. You just need a specific problem to solve and a willingness to learn one tool deeply. Whether you’re looking to pay off debt, save for a trip, or eventually replace your full-time income, the tech space offers more leverage than almost any other industry. A single hour of work can generate value for hundreds of people. A single digital product can sell while you sleep.

But here’s the catch: most people waste months trying to learn everything before they start. They buy courses on Python, web development, and blockchain all at once. They never ship anything. This post is the opposite. I’m going to give you five specific, proven tech side hustles you can start this week. Each one includes a real example, a clear first step, and the exact tools you’ll need.

Let’s cut the noise.

Why Tech Side Hustles Are Different

Most side hustles trade time for money. You wash a car, you get paid. You walk a dog, you get paid. That’s fine, but it caps your earning potential at your physical availability.

Tech side hustles break that ceiling. A single automation script can save a client 20 hours a month. A well-designed Notion template can be sold to 1,000 people. A freelance website project can lead to a retainer that pays you for three hours of maintenance each month. The work scales, and your skills compound. The more you build, the faster you get. The faster you get, the more you can charge.

Plus, the demand is real. Small businesses, solopreneurs, and even large corporations are desperate for people who can make technology work without a 200-page manual. They don’t need a full-time hire. They need someone who can fix a broken email workflow, build a simple landing page, or clean up a messy spreadsheet. That someone can be you.

1. No-Code Automation Specialist

What It Is

You help businesses automate repetitive tasks using tools like Zapier, Make (formerly Integromat), or n8n. Think of it as digital plumbing. A real estate agent wants new leads from their Facebook ad to automatically go into a Google Sheet and trigger a text message. A coach wants their Calendly bookings to create a Trello card and send a welcome email. You build those connections.

Real Example

Sarah, a former teacher, started offering “automation audits” on Upwork. She would spend 30 minutes looking at a small business owner’s workflow, then propose three automations that would save them time. Her first client was a wedding photographer who spent two hours each week manually sending invoice reminders. Sarah built a Zap that did it in zero seconds. She charged $150. The photographer was thrilled. Within six months, Sarah had a waitlist and was charging $500 per project.

Actionable Tips

  • Start with one platform. Master Zapier first. It’s the most popular and has the most integrations.
  • Find your niche. Don’t try to automate everything. Focus on real estate agents, coaches, or e-commerce stores. Learn their specific pain points.
  • Offer a “free audit.” Go on LinkedIn or Facebook groups for small business owners. Offer to look at one of their workflows for free. If you find an automation opportunity, show them the value. Then quote a price.
  • Tools to learn: Zapier, Make, Google Sheets, Airtable.

2. Selling Digital Templates and Notion Setups

What It Is

You design and sell pre-built templates for productivity tools like Notion, Google Sheets, or Canva. People will pay for a system that saves them setup time. A student might buy a Notion dashboard for tracking assignments. A freelancer might pay for an invoice tracker in Google Sheets. A content creator might want a Canva template pack for Instagram stories.

Real Example

Jake was a college student who built a Notion template to track his job applications. He shared it on Reddit, and 200 people asked him for a copy. He cleaned it up, added a tutorial video, and listed it on Gumroad for $19. That week, he made $3,800. He now runs a small store with 15 templates and earns a consistent $2,000 per month in passive income.

Actionable Tips

  • Solve a specific problem. Don’t build a “general productivity template.” Build a “meal planning template for busy moms” or a “content calendar for solo podcasters.”
  • Use Gumroad or Etsy. Gumroad takes a small cut but handles delivery and payments. Etsy has built-in traffic.
  • Make it beautiful but functional. People buy with their eyes first. Spend time on layout and color. Use a clean font.
  • Include a video walkthrough. This reduces refund requests and increases perceived value.
  • Tools to learn: Notion, Google Sheets, Canva, Figma (for design).

3. Freelance Website Maintenance

What It Is

Many small businesses have a website but no one to update it. They need plugin updates, security checks, broken link fixes, or simple content changes like swapping a photo or updating a price. They don’t want to hire an agency. They want a reliable person they can text.

Real Example

Carlos started offering website maintenance to local restaurants. He charged $75 per month for a “basic care” package: weekly backups, plugin updates, and one hour of content changes. He found his first client by walking into a pizza shop that had a broken “order online” button. He fixed it on the spot for free. The owner hired him that week. Carlos now manages 30 sites and earns $2,250 per month in recurring revenue.

Actionable Tips

  • Start with WordPress. It powers over 40% of the web. You only need to know how to update plugins, change text, and manage backups.
  • Offer a free “health check.” Use a tool like GTmetrix or Pingdom to show a business owner their site speed score. Offer to fix one issue for free. Then pitch your monthly plan.
  • Create three tiers. Basic ($50-75/mo for updates and backups), Standard ($100-150/mo plus monthly content changes), Premium ($200-300/mo with SEO tweaks and analytics reports).
  • Tools to learn: WordPress, Elementor (page builder), UpdraftPlus (backups), Google Search Console.

4. AI Prompt Engineering for Small Teams

What It Is

You help people use AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, or Midjourney effectively. Most people type a bad prompt, get a bad result, and give up. You learn how to craft prompts that produce useful, accurate outputs. Then you sell that skill as a service or a product.

Real Example

Mia, a freelance writer, noticed that her clients were struggling to use ChatGPT for social media captions. She created a “Prompt Pack” with 50 tested prompts for Instagram, LinkedIn, and Twitter. She sold it for $27 on Gumroad. She also offered a one-hour consulting session where she taught a small business owner how to use AI for their email newsletters. She charges $150 per session.

Actionable Tips

  • Build a library of prompts. Start with one niche (e.g., real estate listings, fitness content, or lesson plans for teachers). Test each prompt until it consistently produces good results.
  • Sell prompt packs or templates. Use Gumroad or Payhip. Include instructions on how to customize them.
  • Offer “AI onboarding” to small teams. Many small businesses have purchased ChatGPT subscriptions but don’t use them. You can show them how to automate customer service responses, draft blog posts, or summarize meeting notes.
  • Tools to learn: ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Midjourney.

5. Low-Code App Building with Glide or Bubble

What It Is

You build simple mobile apps or web apps without writing traditional code. Platforms like Glide (for internal tools and simple apps) and Bubble (for more complex web apps) let you drag and drop components. You can build a client portal, a booking app, or a habit tracker.

Real Example

Tom, a project manager, built a simple app for a local gym to track member check-ins and class bookings using Glide. The gym had been using paper sign-in sheets. Tom’s app replaced that in two days. He charged $800 for the build and $50 per month for hosting and support. He now has 12 similar clients, all local service businesses.

Actionable Tips

  • Focus on internal tools. Businesses need apps for inventory tracking, employee scheduling, or customer management. These don’t need to be in the App Store.
  • Learn Glide first. It’s easier than Bubble and perfect for data-driven apps that connect to Google Sheets.
  • Find a client before you build. Ask local businesses, “What’s one process you wish you could do on your phone?” If they have a clear answer, you have a project.
  • Tools to learn: Glide, Bubble, Airtable, Google Sheets.

How to Choose the Right Hustle for You

You don’t need to try all five. In fact, that’s a recipe for burnout. Here’s a simple framework:

  • If you love organizing and efficiency: Go with automation specialist or digital templates.
  • If you enjoy fixing things and helping people: Go with website maintenance.
  • If you’re curious about AI and writing: Go with prompt engineering.
  • If you like building visual products: Go with low-code app building.

Pick one. Dedicate two weeks to learning the basics and landing your first client or making your first sale. Don’t worry about perfection. Your first Zapier automation will have a bug. Your first Notion template will be ugly. That’s fine. Ship it, get feedback, improve.

The First Step (Do This Today)

Stop reading. Open a new tab. Go to Gumroad or Etsy and search for “Notion template” or “Zapier automation.” Look at what’s selling. Look at the reviews. What are people complaining about? What’s missing? That’s your idea.

Or, open LinkedIn and search for “small business owner” in your city. Send three of them a message: “I’m starting a side hustle helping small businesses save time with simple tech. Would you be open to a free 15-minute audit of one of your workflows?”

You’ll get ignored by two. One will say yes. That one is your start.

The tech side hustle landscape is wide open. The barrier to entry has never been lower. The only thing stopping you is the belief that you need to be an expert before you start. You don’t. You just need to be one step ahead of the person you’re helping.

Go be that step.

item.title: Best Books to Read in 2025: Curated Picks for Every Reader
item.description: Looking for the best books to read in 2025? Our curated list of fiction, non-fiction, and self-development reads plus simple habits to help you read more.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

A few years ago, I was the person with a nightstand full of unread books and a ready excuse about being too busy. A friend changed that by handing me a worn thriller and saying, “Just ten pages before sleep. No pressure.” That one tiny habit turned me into a 47-book-a-year reader—and I haven’t looked back.

2025 is already a rich year for reading, with fresh releases and rediscovered backlist titles sparking conversations everywhere. In this post, I’ve curated the books that are genuinely worth your precious downtime, covering fiction, non-fiction, and self-development. I’ll also share the practical, no-fuss habits that helped me read consistently without stealing hours from my day. Let’s dive in.

The Best Fiction Books to Read in 2025

For Literary Depth: Tom Lake by Ann Patchett

On a Michigan cherry farm, Lara tells her daughters about the summer she spent acting and a fleeting Hollywood romance. Patchett’s warmth and her sharp insight into
